quest_007_00.story:
At the edge of silver well gardens, Lin Wei waits until the last lantern is lit before speaking. Lin Wei is known as a copper engineer, but that title has become a shelter for a different kind of work. Tonight Lin Wei has brought the lotus seed reliquary, wrapped in cloth that smells of rain. Its marks connect a sister erased from the academy rolls to the curse spreading through Moonwell. Lin Wei asks Lin Yue to examine the evidence before deciding whom to blame.

The first mark is a narrow cut across the relic's underside. Lin Wei explains that official records call it damage, while local witnesses call it a signature. A person trying to hide a name would cut deeper; a person trying to preserve one would cut exactly this far. The distinction matters in Moonwell, where a well that answers only the questions people regret. Lin Yue turns the object toward the light and sees that someone has repaired it more than once.

Qiao Jin remembers the night differently. Qiao Jin heard a bell before the storm and a second bell after the soldiers departed. Between those sounds, the courtyard filled with people carrying sealed letters. None were allowed to read what they delivered. The moon covenant later claimed that every messenger had volunteered. Lin Wei wants their consent investigated, because a promise made under threat cannot become a sacred oath merely by surviving long enough to be written down.

This chapter is called A Name in Water. Its immediate task is speak with Lin Wei. That is a practical beginning rather than a complete answer: the mountain cannot be cured by a single sword stroke, and a village cannot be reconciled by declaring one witness pure. Lin Yue agrees to return with a result that can be checked. Lin Wei insists that neither impressive qi nor an imperial title will substitute for evidence gathered in the living world.

The road to Thunder Pass follows an old route used by patients, refugees, and tax collectors. Its stones carry shallow footprints that rain has not erased. Lin Wei gives Lin Yue a simple rule for the journey: stop whenever a voice offers certainty without a cost. Spirits on this road repeat bargains they barely understood when they were alive. Their answers are useful only when compared with the ordinary details their promises leave behind.

By the roadside, Lin Yue finds a small offering bowl. Someone has placed fresh water beside an old piece of charcoal, a gesture that seems contradictory until Qiao Jin explains it. The water is for those who survived; the charcoal is for those whose names were burned. Both offerings belong at the same table. Removing one to make the shrine look harmonious would repeat the choice that damaged Moonwell in the first place.

The creature called Ink Raven appears in three different accounts of the disaster. Soldiers described it as a punishment, merchants as a profitable omen, and children as something that stood between them and the fire. Its behavior now follows the pattern of leech. The pattern gives Lin Yue a tactical warning, but it also suggests that the creature remembers a command. A monster can become dangerous while carrying a duty that nobody has released.

Lin Wei once trusted the moon covenant because its members promised to protect people without demanding that they become useful first. That promise was tested when food ran short. The council began measuring every household by its ability to repay aid. Those who could not repay were called disloyal. The relic passed through this accounting system and came back with one mark missing. Lin Yue must decide whether the missing mark is an accident or a deliberate erasure.

At an abandoned rest station, a caretaker keeps two copies of the same testimony. One is clean enough for an archive; the other contains corrections made by the people who were present. The clean copy is easier to read and wrong in six important places. Qiao Jin asks Lin Yue to take both. Destroying the polished lie might satisfy anger, but preserving the comparison gives future readers a way to recognize the method of the deception.

The next clue concerns a sister erased from the academy rolls. Lin Wei has told this part of their history so often that listeners mistake its careful wording for detachment. Lin Wei chooses each word because careless listeners have used their grief as permission to punish strangers. Lin Yue lets the account remain unfinished. A witness does not owe an audience a satisfying conclusion before her evidence can be believed, and the absence of a neat ending does not make the loss less real.

The relic's qi changes near silver well gardens. It does not become stronger; it becomes more specific. A loose vibration resolves into the rhythm of a familiar working song. Lin Wei recognizes the song because they learned it before they learned to cultivate. Its final verse names a place the official map omits. Lin Yue records the verse instead of immediately following it. A map can be incomplete without every omission being a trap, but this omission has acquired too many guards.

When Lin Yue considers the fighting ahead, she remembers Master Shen's distinction between power and cultivation. Power can interrupt an enemy's body. Cultivation should also interrupt the habit of treating interruption as an answer. Against Ink Raven, that means observing the warning motion before committing to a strike, keeping a route back to the lanterns, and leaving enough stamina to withdraw. A victory that strands the witness beside a new danger would fail the purpose of the chapter.

Qiao Jin proposes an easy solution: give the relic to the strongest sect and let its authority settle the dispute. Lin Wei refuses without accusing the witness of cowardice. Easy solutions become attractive when every difficult solution has already charged a person too much. The refusal therefore needs an alternative. Lin Yue offers to separate the immediate threat from the long argument, so that nobody has to remain in danger merely to preserve the appearance of patience.

That alternative requires attention to ordinary supplies. Moonlotus is gathered because roots hold a memory of clean water; jade essence is studied because its vibration can distinguish a binding from a natural current. Neither material is miraculous by itself. Lin Wei teaches Lin Yue to describe what was collected, where it was found, and what changed after contact. The lesson makes a record useful to people who do not share the cultivator's instincts or her access to rare techniques.

A messenger from Thunder Pass arrives with a request to postpone the work. The request is polite, detailed, and unsigned. Its language praises duty without cruelty while asking everyone affected by the curse to wait in silence. Lin Yue notices that no date is offered for a new hearing. Qiao Jin has learned to fear indefinite patience more than open threats. They agree to continue the practical task while keeping the message as another piece of evidence.

During a quiet interval, Lin Wei speaks about the life she wanted before the disaster. They wanted time to practice their trade well enough that nobody would remember them as extraordinary. The mountain's crisis has turned every useful act into a test of allegiance. Lin Yue understands the exhaustion in that change. A just ending should give people permission to return to ordinary ambitions, rather than replacing one eternal duty with another whose keeper merely has a kinder face.

The danger returns when Ink Raven senses movement near the old boundary. Its first approach is a warning, its second a commitment. Lin Yue must meet the actual threat rather than the reputation built around it. She watches its distance, keeps the witnesses outside the line of attack, and uses the terrain to break pursuit. The task of speak with Lin Wei cannot be completed by claiming a kill or a delivery that the world has not actually registered.

The creature has a particular history: The ink on its wings comes from unsent pardon letters hidden beneath the executioner's desk.
quest_007_00.aftermath:
After the immediate work, Qiao Jin asks what should happen to the people who benefited from the lie. Lin Wei gives a difficult answer: protection should end where it becomes immunity, but blame should stop where the evidence stops. Lin Yue can favor restitution without promising that everyone will be forgiven. She can favor judgment without declaring that the descendants of an offender inherit the offense. The chapter leaves room for both courage and limits.

The lotus seed reliquary now carries enough context to be read as more than a treasure. Its value lies in the relationships it documents: who asked for aid, who supplied it, who altered the terms, and who paid after the agreement was changed. Lin Wei wants a copy placed somewhere ordinary people can reach. An archive behind a sect's locked gate might preserve the truth while returning ownership of it to the institution that first concealed it.

Lin Yue returns through silver well gardens with the result of speak with Lin Wei. The lantern keeper does not ask how dramatic the journey became. She asks whether the expected evidence arrived and whether anyone must still be searched for. That question sets the measure of success. Lin Wei records the chapter beside the earlier ones, so that later choices will be judged against the whole sequence rather than the most flattering moment in the cultivator's account.

Before the next chapter begins, Lin Wei offers a conversation rather than another command. Lin Wei asks Lin Yue whether duty without cruelty can survive when it ceases to look heroic. They compare the answer with the fate of Immortal Xu, whose wish to protect his daughter became a binding on an entire mountain. Neither woman treats his grief as a crime. They examine the moment when he decided that grief granted him ownership of someone else's future.

The closing note is deliberately provisional. In Moonwell, the immediate task has a measurable result, but the meaning of that result belongs to more than one person. Qiao Jin receives a copy, Lin Wei retains another, and Lin Yue carries the route onward. At the end of the twelve-chapter arc, she will choose whether to release the relic's binding or keep its strength. Until then, the work is to make that choice informed rather than inevitable.
quest_007_00.mercy: Lin Wei records the result of the task to speak with Lin Wei. The account is witnessed rather than final: Qiao Jin receives a copy, and the next chapter follows the evidence carried by the lotus seed reliquary. The binding's final fate remains undecided.

Lin Yue can favor restitution without promising that everyone will be forgiven. She can favor judgment without declaring that the descendants of an offender inherit the offense. The chapter leaves room for both courage and limits.

The jade examination tile now carries enough context to be read as more than a treasure. Its value lies in the relationships it documents: who asked for aid, who supplied it, who altered the terms, and who paid after the agreement was changed. Zhao Xuan wants a copy placed somewhere ordinary people can reach. An archive behind a sect's locked gate might preserve the truth while returning ownership of it to the institution that first concealed it.

Lin Yue returns through silver well gardens with the result of defeat 1 manifestation of Mist Jellyfish. The lantern keeper does not ask how dramatic the journey became. She asks whether the expected evidence arrived and whether anyone must still be searched for. That question sets the measure of success. Zhao Xuan records the chapter beside the earlier ones, so that later choices will be judged against the whole sequence rather than the most flattering moment in the cultivator's account.

As the final chapter closes, Zhao Xuan offers a conversation rather than another command. Zhao Xuan asks Lin Yue whether mercy without obedience can survive when it ceases to look heroic. They compare the answer with the fate of Immortal Xu, whose wish to protect his daughter became a binding on an entire mountain. Neither woman treats his grief as a crime. They examine the moment when he decided that grief granted him ownership of someone else's future.

The closing note is deliberately provisional. In Moonwell, the immediate task has a measurable result, but the meaning of that result belongs to more than one person. Mei Lian receives a copy, Zhao Xuan retains another, and Lin Yue carries the route onward. With the twelve-chapter investigation complete, she can now choose whether to release the relic's binding or keep its strength. The evidence makes this final choice informed rather than inevitable.
quest_091_11.mercy: Zhao Xuan releases the jade examination tile from its binding. Her final account favors mercy without obedience, and Moonwell gains a witness rather than another immortal keeper.
quest_091_11.power: Zhao Xuan entrusts the jade examination tile to Lin Yue. Its strength remains useful, but the final account records the obligation carried by every person whose memory powers it.
